K.title: A long-ago tool
K.text: People used to write with feathers dipped in ink. Draw or write what that might have looked like.

K.title: The first day of school, then
K.text: Imagine a kid going to school 100 years ago. Tell what happens first, next, and last.

1.title: The day the lights came on
1.text: Long ago many homes had no electric lights. Write two facts about how people saw at night, then tell what you think about that.

1.title: If I met a history helper
1.text: Write a short letter to a firefighter, nurse, or teacher from long ago. Thank them and ask one question.

2.title: A day that changed a town
2.text: Pick a real event from this week in history. Tell the story of one kid who was there.

2.title: Should we still study this?
2.text: Pick a person from history. Write whether kids should still learn about them, and give two reasons.

3.title: Today in history
3.text: Choose something that happened on this date. Explain what happened, who was there, and why it still matters.

3.title: Letter to the past
3.text: Write a letter to a child who lived 150 years ago. Tell them one thing about your life and ask about theirs.

4.title: A turning point
4.text: Explain a historical turning point in three parts: what life was like before, what changed, and what came next.

4.title: Who belongs in the story?
4.text: Should history class include more ordinary kids and families, not only famous leaders? Take a side and support it.

5.title: Cause and effect
5.text: Pick a historical event. Explain at least two causes and two effects, using linking words.

5.title: Monument argument
5.text: A town wants a new monument. Argue what it should honor and why.

6.title: Primary source detective
6.text: Imagine you found a diary page from this week in history. Explain what a historian could learn from it, and what they still would not know.

6.title: Was it worth it?
6.text: Choose a hard choice a historical figure made. Argue whether it was worth the cost.

7.title: Then and now
7.text: Compare a right, job, or daily habit from the past with today. Explain what changed and what did not.

7.title: Rewrite the headline
7.text: Take a historical event often told one way. Argue for another way of telling it, using reasons and evidence.

8.title: Civic memory
8.text: Explain how a community remembers a historical event (holiday, monument, story) and what that memory leaves out.

8.title: Policy from the past
8.text: Should a past law or policy be studied as a warning, a model, or both? Argue your claim.

K.title: A weird animal trick
K.text: Pick an animal that does something odd. Tell one thing it does and why that might help it.

1.title: Why is the sky that color?
1.text: Write what you notice about the sky and one idea for why it looks that way.

2.title: If I shrank
2.text: Write a story about shrinking to the size of an ant for one hour. What do you notice?

3.title: Strange but true
3.text: Explain a surprising science fact. Include what happens, why scientists think it happens, and one example.

3.title: Should we try it?
3.text: Scientists want to try a wild experiment (growing food on a roof, a robot class pet). Should they? Give reasons.

4.title: How it works
4.text: Explain how a simple system works (the water cycle, a seed becoming a plant, a flashlight).

5.title: Claim from evidence
5.text: Make a claim about a science question (Do we need more recess outside?). Support it with facts a reader can check.

6.title: Design a test
6.text: Describe a fair test for a question you care about. Name the variable, what you would measure, and what would count as evidence.

7.title: Systems thinking
7.text: Pick a system (a wetland, a city power grid, your own body). Explain how parts work together and what happens if one part fails.

8.title: Science in public
8.text: Should a new technology (AI homework helper, gene editing, space mining) be allowed for kids your age? Argue with reasons and limits.

K.title: Dear someone I love
K.text: Write or dictate a letter to a family member. Tell them one thing you did today.

1.title: Thank-you note
1.text: Write a thank-you letter. Name the person, the thing they did, and how it made you feel.

2.title: Please and why
2.text: Write a letter asking a grown-up for something you want. Give two fair reasons.

3.title: News from camp
3.text: Write a letter home about a real or imagined day. Include something funny, something hard, and a question.

3.title: Letter to a hero
3.text: Write to someone who helps your town. Tell what you notice and ask one thoughtful question.

4.title: Family history ask
4.text: Write to a relative asking about a story from their childhood. Explain why you want to know.

5.title: The case for a change
5.text: Write a persuasive letter to a principal, coach, or parent asking for one change. Use reasons and a respectful tone.

6.title: Two audiences
6.text: Write a letter to a younger kid explaining a family tradition. Then add a P.S. to an adult with a different detail.

7.title: Open letter
7.text: Write an open letter about a community issue. Name the audience, the problem, and one action you want.

8.title: Letter across time
8.text: Write to your future self at 18. Tell them what you believe now, what you are working on, and what you hope they remember.

K.title: I found this
K.text: Tell about something you found outside or in a book. What is it? What is odd about it?

1.title: A tiny discovery
1.text: Write about a time you noticed something small that other people missed.

2.title: Wait, that's real?
2.text: Explain a surprising discovery (a deep-sea animal, a planet, a cave). Give two facts.

3.title: Outrageous but true
3.text: Pick a wild discovery. Explain what people thought before, what was found, and why it matters.

3.title: Should we look closer?
3.text: Is it better to explore space, the ocean, or the past next? Pick one and defend it.

4.title: How they knew
4.text: Explain how a scientist, explorer, or kid inventor knew they had found something new.

5.title: The cost of finding out
5.text: Some discoveries are risky or expensive. Argue when the search is still worth it.

6.title: Failed then famous
6.text: Tell the story of a discovery that started as a mistake. Sequence the attempts and the turning point.

7.title: What counts as proof
7.text: Explain how a discovery moved from a hunch to something people could trust.

8.title: Who gets credit
8.text: Many discoveries involved more than one person. Argue how credit should be shared, using a real example.
